title: Effect of performance level on pacing strategy during a 10-km running race
authors: Lima-Silva AE, Bertuzzi RC, Pires FO, Barros RV, Gagliardi JF, Hammond J, Kiss MA, Bishop DJ
population: 24 male runners in a self-paced treadmill 10-km trial, split into terciles by performance (high and low groups compared)
findings: In the high-performing group velocity peaked at 18.8 +/- 1.4 km/h in the first 400 m, above the average race velocity; this was not different from the low group's average racing velocity (14.5 +/- 0.7 km/h).
Velocity then fell non-significantly until 9,600 m, followed by an increase at the end (P < 0.05).
High and low performance runners adopted different pacing strategies; peak treadmill velocity, running economy and lactate threshold correlated with start, middle, last and average velocity.
limitations: 24 men on a treadmill, not a road race; terciles of one small sample; the low group's strategy is not described in the abstract beyond 'different'.
implications: Laboratory 10 km pacing: a fast opening then a slow drift and an end spurt in better runners. It does not support a prescribed 10 km split pattern. Kept as the 10 km counterpart of the road-race pacing records, with the limit that it is a treadmill study.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (online 2009-12-11, print volume 108, 2010; the stored year follows the print volume, within Crossref's one-year tolerance). Abstract read on Europe PMC. Crossref lists no correction, erratum or retraction notice (checked 2026-11-16).
